article.title: Why Average Customer Value Can Mislead a Business
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
Managers often summarize customers with an average: average order value, average monthly revenue, or average number of purchases. Averages are convenient because they compress thousands of observations into one number. The problem is that a stable or improving average can hide important changes in the customer base.

Imagine an online service with two groups. Most customers pay $20 per month, while a small group of enterprise customers pays $500. If several ordinary customers leave but one enterprise customer joins, average revenue per customer may rise. A dashboard could therefore show a positive trend even though the company is losing many relationships.

The same problem appears when customer behavior is highly skewed. A few very large purchases can pull the mean upward. The ‘average customer’ described by the metric may barely exist in reality. Looking at the median and the distribution can reveal whether growth is broad or concentrated among a small number of accounts.

Mix changes are another source of confusion. Suppose a retailer reduces promotions for low-value shoppers and attracts more premium customers. Average order value rises, but that does not necessarily mean existing customers are spending more. The customer mix has changed. This may be an excellent strategy, but managers should identify the mechanism correctly before copying it elsewhere.

Cohort analysis helps. Instead of combining everyone, analysts can group customers by acquisition month, product, channel, region, or segment and follow their behavior over time. They can ask whether customers acquired in May retain better than those acquired in January, or whether the same customers are increasing their spending.

Weighted averages require similar care. A company-wide satisfaction score can improve because a high-scoring segment became larger, even if satisfaction fell inside every segment. This is a composition effect. The aggregate number is mathematically correct but can support the wrong business story.

For decision-making, managers should pair averages with diagnostic questions. How wide is the distribution? What does the median show? Are a few customers driving the result? Has the mix of segments changed? What happens within comparable cohorts? Is the metric calculated per active customer, per registered customer, or per transaction?

Time windows matter too. A monthly average may rise because seasonal customers disappear from the denominator, while a yearly view tells a different story. Analysts should keep definitions stable and compare like with like. When definitions change, dashboards should make the break visible instead of presenting the series as continuous.

None of this means averages are bad. They are useful summaries and often belong on executive dashboards. The mistake is treating the summary as an explanation. An average tells you where the center of a dataset is under a particular definition; it does not tell you why the number moved.

A strong analysis therefore moves from aggregate to decomposition. Start with the headline average, then separate changes caused by customer behavior from changes caused by customer composition. That extra step can turn a comforting metric into a more accurate picture of growth, retention, and risk.
paragraphs.zh: 平均客戶價值很方便，但可能掩蓋客群組成變化。少數高價值客戶就可能把平均數拉高，即使大量一般客戶正在流失。分析時應搭配 median、distribution、cohort 與 segment mix，並確認指標分母和時間窗是否一致。平均數適合當摘要，但不能直接當成原因。
paragraphs.ja: 平均顧客価値は便利ですが、顧客構成の変化を隠すことがあります。少数の高額顧客によって平均が上昇しても、多くの一般顧客が離脱している可能性があります。median、distribution、cohort、segment mixを併用し、定義や期間も揃える必要があります。
